name: Mangap-Mbula
confidence_why: Bugenhagen's 1995 reference grammar sets out a full rule system for Mangap-Mbula stress (initial by default, pulled onto a following long vowel or vowel cluster, verb subject prefixes skipped), and the only dissent is the same author's one-sentence 1992 phonology data sheet saying stress is penultimate, a draft summary that gives the same result as the grammar in disyllables and in words with a long penult.
catalog_citation: Bugenhagen, Robert D. 1995. A grammar of Mangap-Mbula: an Austronesian language of Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics C-101. Canberra: ANU. (open access, hdl 1885/145877)
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.6 'Stress placement', pp. 76-80 (pp. 90-94; Rules 39-43: Initial Stress Placement, Stress Attraction to Following Vocoid Clusters o…
catalog_quote: Word-level stress differences are not particularly pronounced in Mangap-Mbula. ... The placement of stress is predictable, but several interacting rules are required. In most words, primary stress falls on the initial syllable: [mólo] long [mólolo] long (of plural objects) [bá:da] you (SG) carry [mútu] island ... [tómtom] person [pósop] you (SG) finish ... The Subject prefixes on verbs, however, are extrametrical ... The first of these adjustments shifts stress to a following vocoid cluster or lengthened vocoid, if one is present. It is evidenced by forms like the following ones: [kumbú:nu] 3SG leg ... [tomó:to] man, male [ikokóu] 3SG be white [aŋgaráu] I approach ... The vast majority of stems in the language are three syllables or less in length and are accounted for by the above three rules. ... syllables of a word are grouped into two syllable rhythmic clusters (termed 'Feet'), begi…

new_statements.locator: p. 4, section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' (PDF printed 'August 26, 2004', 5 pp; the sentence is the whole section)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: the PDF's metadata gives the Title 'OPD', Subject 'Mangap-Mbula', SIL PNG Branch, Distiller 2004) and re-ran extracted text on p. 4. The section heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' is followed by exactly the two sentences quoted: 'The placement of stress is predictable. In most words, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable.' Nothing else in the section; no tone or weight statement anywhere; p. 3 says long vowels 'are analyzed as vowel sequences'; example words and the transcribed passage (pp. 4-5) carry no stress marks; the Syllable Patterns table lists only CV shapes. Reading fixed: penultimate syllable with the 'in most words' hedge is correct; no secondary stress,…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Mangap-Mbula exists but has an empty rule and there are no existing statements; this source supplies the placement (penultimate, predictable) that the catalog record lacks. The digital copy is the Internet Archive copy (2024-09-10) of the PDF the SIL Archives 42432 landing page links to; the landing page is live (HTTP 200, 2026-09-17) and links the same PDF path, but the PDF itself could not be reached by automated download on both attempts, so the archived copy is the one read.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable, not lexical; primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word in most words. No tone is described (the 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' heading is the SIL OPD template, and only stress is filled); vowel length exists but is analysed as vowel sequences, so no weight rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'In most words'; no exceptions are listed or exemplified, and no stress marks appear in the example words or the transcribed text.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD is headed 'Mangap-Mbula (Mangaaba, Mangaaba-Mbula, Mangap) Language [MNA], Semo – Morobe Province', major villages Yangla and Kampalap; it does not name a dialect for the stress statement. The 2007 dictionary (same author, held by the project) says its data largely reflects the Central dialect (Yangla) and that four dialects exist (Gauru, Central, Northern, Sakar), differing in vowel length and /nz/ vs /z/; nothing there ties stress to a dialect.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation and locator (Bugenhagen 1995 PL C-101, sec. 2.6 pp. 76-80, Rules 39-43) are confirmed verbatim in the text file we hold. (2) Deciding source is the standard 418-pp Pacific Linguistics reference grammar by the long-term SIL fieldworker, Glottolog's top descriptive reference and the only grammar of the language; its stress section is a full rule system with derivations, and the 'weight' coding (Rule 40: stress attracted off the default initial syllable onto a following long vowel / vocoid cluster, e.g. [tomó:to] vs [mútu]) is exactly what pp. 77-78 say. that gap is stated, not papered over).
